With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?ByDaniel Bush
Washington correspondentPublished5 November 2026, 02:33 GMTUpdated 03:47 GMT
Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.
In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.
But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.

Could Democrats in Congress end the war in Iran?
Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.
"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.

item.title: France holds new strikes and protests as unions demand immediate answers
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
The head of France's CGT labour union, Sophie Binet (C), said the wave of protests and strikes had reached a new levelByPaul KirbyEurope digital editorPublished5 November 2026, 09:34 GMTUpdated 52 minutes ago
Protests are taking place across France after five unions launched a national day of strike action, joining high school students and demonstrators criticising the rising cost of living.
More than 250,000 people had taken to the streets in almost 70 towns and cities by 13:00 (12:00 GMT) on Thursday, and that was "just the start", said Sophie Binet of the CGT union.
The unions have vowed to take the wave of protests that began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycées (high schools) "to the next level".
They have since spread to include workers and the so-called "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 70,000 police were being deployed, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.
Some unrest has been reported in the cities of Lyon and Rennes.
A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the Rhône river in central Lyon, as hundreds of people belonging to the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.
Meanwhile, there were clashes in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march.
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
A car was set alight during a protest in the centre of Lyon
The five unions have combined forces across the public and private sector, announcing more than 250 separate actions as part of their campaign for higher wages to combat the cost of living and protect public services.
Binet told reporters at the start of a march in central Paris that protesters had "just reached a new level in their mobilisation" and were demanding immediate answers.

item.title: Russell Brand is being investigated over two new rape complaints, police say
item.description:
Image source, Zeynep Demir/Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault, following a three-week trial at Southwark Crown Court ByHelena WilkinsonNews correspondentPublished5 November 2026, 15:02 GMTUpdated 51 minutes ago
Warning: Details of rape and sexual assault
Russell Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women, it can now be reported.
The disgraced comedian has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault by a jury of eight men and four women at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.
More victims are likely to come forward following his conviction, the detective who led the police investigation has said.
Det Supt Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police, said he hoped other women would gain "courage" and "confidence" from the guilty verdicts.
Brand was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
'Ruthless'
Brand had initially been coy and quiet in police interviews, said Furphy, but became bolder as officers continued to question him.
"As he gets used to something, he becomes more emboldened by it," Furphy said. "You can certainly see that in his offending."
Hundreds of people were interviewed as part of the investigation and officers said several witnesses came forward, some of whom had previously had a sexual relationship with Brand. Katy Perry, the US singer who was married to Brand from 2010 to 2012, was not interviewed.
Brand, 51, who was described in court as "ruthless" and a "sexual predator", was once one of the UK's most high-profile and in-demand entertainers.
Some of the women said they had been left "haunted for years" by what he did to them.
Speaking to the BBC, officers working on the three-year Metropolitan Police investigation described how bringing Brand to justice was not without its challenges.

Italian chef Davide Tamburella was fired from a Brisbane restaurant in May after the establishment's management expressed concerns about a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function.
It was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
At the time, the chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".

item.title: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules
item.description:
Image source, HBO Max/Warner BrosImage caption,
Noah Wyle stars in The Pitt, the medical series set in a Pittsburgh emergency room that first aired in 2025 BySteven McIntoshEntertainment reporter Published5 hours ago
US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled.
The widow of Michael Crichton, who created ER, argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the series, which has been made without proper permission or credit.
Sherri Crichton says her husband's contract included a "frozen rights" provision that prohibited any spin-offs, sequels or reboots of ER being made without his express consent.
A three-judge panel said there are "clear and numerous similarities between The Pitt and ER," which means the case can go ahead. Warner Bros previously described the lawsuit as "baseless" and sought to have it dismissed.
Listing the similarities between the two shows, the court cited the emergency room setting, the fast pace, use of medical jargon, graphic depictions of injuries, and younger doctors fresh from medical school being trained.
"We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case," the judges said.
It means the case will now go to a jury trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.
But the judges dismissed separate claims against actor-producer Noah Wyle, executive producer John Wells and showrunner R Scott Gemmill.
The justices said there was insufficient evidence to show the three producers were aware they could be violating Crichton's contractual rights.
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Noah Wyle (second right) previously starred in ER alongside Anthony Edwards, George Clooney and Eriq La Salle
ER launched in 1994, based on original screenplay written by Crichton. It starred George Clooney, Anthony Edwards, Eriq La Salle and Maria Bello, and aired 331 episodes over the next 15 years.

item.title: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: Hong Kong pro-democracy advocate Joshua Wong jailed for 10 yearsByAbel U, BBC Chinese, Reporting fromHong Kong and Kelly NgPublished5 November 2026, 03:08 GMTUpdated 2 hours ago
Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law.
Wong is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control.
Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy.
Having already spent the last six years in jail, Wong, who was due to be freed in January, will now spend another decade behind bars.
Silenced and erased, Hong Kong's decade of protest is now a defiant memory
Published30 November 2024
What a defiant mogul's trial says about Hong Kong
Published18 December 2023
Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was in his early teens.
On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, to which he pleaded guilty in Sep...

item.title: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Fishermen return to sea under a crimson sky in August after China's Jiangsu province is hit by Super Typhoon DolphinByJoel Guinto, Reporting fromSingapore, Kurumi Mori, Tokyo correspondent and Darren Bett, Lead weather presenterPublished4 November 2026
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi,...

item.title: Pope Leo hosts Bob Dylan at official residence in Rome
item.description:
Image source, Vatican pool/GettyImage caption,
The two Americans met during Dylan's tour of ItalyByHelen DavidsonPublished5 November 2026, 02:09 GMT
Pope Leo XIV hosted Bob Dylan at his official residence, the Apostolic Palace, on Wednesday during the Rome stop on the singer-songwriter's Italian tour.
Dylan, 85, wore a nearly all-black outfit, including a pulled up hoodie, gloves and umbrella, starkly contrasting with the Chicago-born Pope's all-white vestments.
The meeting between the pair, who both hail from the US Midwest, was brief, according to Vatican News.
Leo presented the Nobel laureate with a rosary and Dylan gifted Leo a copy of his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One.
Image source, Vatican pool/Getty
The visit happened ahead of Dylan's scheduled performance on Thursday at the Palazzo dello Sport as part of his ongoing tour.
Leo has previously referenced Dylan in his own work, quoting Dylan's unreleased anti-nuclear song, Go Away You Bomb, in the preface to a book titled Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift.
"I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled," was the line quoted in the book's warning to the world against rearmament.
The song was written in 1963 amid the Cold War, but was never recorded. The typewritten lyrics were unpublished until 2013 when they were discovered and put up for auction, according to the New York Times.
It was the second time Dylan had met a pope. In 1997 Dylan was invited to perform in front of Pope John Paul II and about 300,000 young people for the 23rd National Eucharistic Congress in Bologna.
Dylan played four songs including Knockin' on Heaven's Door, and reportedly climbed the stage mid-set to greet John Paul with a handshake and exchange a few words.
The then-Pope quoted Dylan's hit Blowin' in the Wind in his sermon to the crowd.

item.title: India's costliest film retells a beloved Hindu epic - but divides critics
item.description:
Image source, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, Sony PicturesImage caption,
The film adapts the revered Hindu epic RamayanaByZoya MateenBBC News, DelhiPublished7 hours ago
India's most expensive film - a lavish retelling of the Hindu epic Ramayana, made in two parts for a reported $500m (£370m) - has opened in cinemas worldwide, sparking enormous expectations and mixed reviews.
Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the first of two planned films, a sprawling production that brings together some of India's biggest stars, Hollywood visual-effects expertise and two Oscar-winning composers in an attempt to take one of the country's most revered stories to a global audience.
One of Hinduism's foundational epics, the Ramayana has travelled across centuries and continents, finding expression in poetry, temple sculpture, shadow puppetry, folk theatre and stories passed down through generations. It has outlasted kingdoms and empires, inspired religious devotion and political movements, and found new life, again and again, on TV and in cinema.
Tiwari's version returns to the familiar story of love, duty, exile and war, set in a world of gods and demons, celestial weapons and mighty kingdoms.
Ranbir Kapoor plays Lord Ram, the virtuous prince of Ayodhya. Banished from his kingdom for 14 years, he retreats to the forest with his wife Sita (played by Sai Pallavi), who is kidnapped by Ravana, the 10-headed king of Lanka.

item.title: Six dead and others injured in fire at New York City building
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
More than 230 fire and emergency medical personnel responded (file photo)ByJames FitzGeraldPublished5 November 2026, 11:54 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
Six people have died after a large fire broke out in a residential building in Brooklyn, New York City, officials say.
Several others were hurt in the blaze, which occurred early on Thursday morning, the New York City Fire Department (FDNY) said in a statement.
More than 230 fire and emergency medical personnel were sent to the scene near Sunset Park after the fire was first reported at around 01:40 local time (06:40 GMT).
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he was "heartbroken" by the deaths, and has asked New Yorkers to "take a moment to pray for the full recovery of those who were injured".
The cause of the blaze is being investigated.
A crew specialising in hazardous materials was sent to the scene because of the presence of a lithium-ion battery, although it was not clear whether this was linked to the blaze.
The emergency responders reportedly discovered on their arrival that the building's first and second floors had been engulfed by flames.
Four individuals were pronounced dead at the scene, according to the FDNY.
A male and female were also taken to the hospital, where they were pronounced dead, the New York City Police Department (NYPD) said.
Six other civilians were injured, two of them critically, along with three firefighters, the FDNY said.
